cues.text: Two armies face each other at dawn, on the field of Kurukshetra.
Between them, in one chariot, stands Arjuna, the finest archer of his age. And his hands begin to shake.
His mouth goes dry. His bow slips from his hand. He sits down in the chariot, and says: I will not fight.
The one holding the reins is Shri Krishna. And Krishna smiles.
Chapter two, verse ten.
Then, O Bharata, between the two armies, Hrishikesha, as if smiling, spoke these words to the one sinking in despair.

Thousands of years later, at one forty-seven in the morning, Meera, twenty-one, stares at two emails. One is the safe job her family is already celebrating. The other is the path she actually wants. She has to reply by morning. And her hands are shaking too.
What Krishna told Arjuna that morning is the Bhagavad Gita: seven hundred verses, eighteen chapters, inside the sixth book of the Mahabharata. Here is all of it, in fifteen minutes.
Many teachers read the eighteen chapters as three movements of six: action, devotion, and knowledge.
Chapter one. The yoga of Arjuna's despair.
Arjuna looks across the field and sees teachers, cousins, his own grandfather. And he breaks.
Even this collapse is called a yoga, because it is where the journey begins.
Verse forty-seven.
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.
Chapter two. The yoga of understanding.
It begins with a surrender. Arjuna says: I am your disciple. Teach me.
Krishna's first lesson is about who Arjuna really is. The self is never born and never dies. As we throw off worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self moves from body to body.
Then comes the most famous line in the Gita. Verse forty-seven.
Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not cling to inaction.
It does not say: don't care about results. It says: don't let results run you.
And the chapter ends with a portrait of a steady mind: not shaken by sorrow, not hungry for pleasure, free of craving, fear and anger.
Chapter three. The yoga of action.
Arjuna asks: if knowing is better than doing, why push me into this terrible act? Krishna answers: no one can stay without acting, even for a moment. So act, but act as an offering.
And remember that people are watching. Whatever the best person does, Krishna says, others copy. Whatever standard they set, the world follows.
And here is a verse for everyone who scrolls through other people's lives. Verse thirty-five.
Better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's dharma done well. Better to die in your own dharma; another's dharma is full of fear.
Chapter four. The yoga of knowledge.
Krishna reveals who he is. He taught this yoga long ago to Vivasvan, the sun, who taught it to Manu, who taught it to Ikshvaku. And he makes a promise. Verses seven and eight.
Whenever dharma declines, O Bharata, and adharma rises, then I bring myself forth. To protect the good, to destroy wrongdoing, and to establish dharma, I come into being, age after age.

How do you find this knowledge? Bow down, ask questions, and serve, Krishna says, and those who have seen the truth will teach you. And as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge burns all karma to ash.
Chapter five. The yoga of renunciation.
Arjuna asks again: which is better, giving up action, or acting well? Both lead to freedom, Krishna says, but acting without attachment is better. Picture a lotus leaf. Verse ten.
One who acts, offering every action to Brahman and giving up attachment, is not stained by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
And the wise, he says, see the same self in a learned scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and the person the world pushes away.
Chapter six. The yoga of self-mastery.
It opens with a line made for two in the morning. Verse five.
Lift yourself up by yourself; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is its enemy.
Meditation here is not escape. Yoga is not for one who eats too much or too little, Krishna says, or who sleeps too much or too little. It is balance.

Arjuna is honest. The mind is restless, he says, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna does not deny it. By practice, and by letting go, it can be held. And a mind that is held is like a lamp in a windless place. It does not flicker.
Meera turns her phone face down. The fear does not leave. But for the first time tonight, she is not fighting her own mind.
The second movement turns to Krishna himself.
Chapter seven. The yoga of knowledge and realisation.
Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego: this, Krishna says, is my lower nature. Life itself is my higher nature. Verse seven.
There is nothing higher than me, Dhananjaya. All this is strung on me, like gems on a thread.
I am the taste in water, he says, the light of the sun and the moon, the sacred syllable Om in all the Vedas.
Chapter eight. The yoga of the imperishable.
Whatever a person remembers at the very end, Krishna says, that is what they reach. So he gives Arjuna the simplest practice in the Gita. Verse seven.
Therefore, at all times, remember me, and fight. With your mind and intellect offered to me, you will surely come to me.
Not: leave the world, then remember. Remember, and do the work in front of you.
Chapter nine. The yoga of the royal secret.
Those who worship me with nothing else in their minds, Krishna says, I carry what they need and protect what they have. That line is the motto on the logo of LIC.
And the royal secret turns out to be gentle. Verse twenty-six.
Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering, made with devotion by one whose heart is pure, I accept and partake of.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, he says, do it as an offering to me.
Chapter ten. The yoga of divine glories.

Arjuna asks: where should I look for you? Among mountains, Krishna says, I am the Himalaya. Among trees, the sacred fig. Among rivers, the Ganga. Among months, Margashirsha, the month of Gita Jayanti. Among seasons, spring. Verse forty-one.
Whatever being is glorious, beautiful or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendour.
Chapter eleven. The vision of the universal form.
This is the summit.

Arjuna asks to see Krishna's cosmic form. You cannot see me with these eyes, Krishna says, so I give you divine sight. And Sanjaya, who is telling the story, tries to describe what Arjuna saw. Verse twelve.
If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth in the sky at once, it might resemble the splendour of that great being.

Arjuna sees every world inside one form, with no beginning, no middle and no end. Warriors rush into it the way rivers rush into the sea. Then Krishna speaks a verse that the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer said came to his mind at the first atomic test. Verse thirty-two.
I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds, come forth to consume the worlds. Even without you, none of the warriors arrayed in the opposing armies will remain.
Terrified, Arjuna begs to see the familiar form again. And Vasudeva, gently, becomes himself once more.
Chapter twelve. The yoga of devotion.
One of the two shortest chapters, just twenty verses.

Who is the better devotee, Arjuna asks: the one who loves a form, or the one who seeks the formless? For people in bodies, Krishna says, the path of love is easier. Then he describes who is dear to him. Verse thirteen.
One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from 'mine' and from ego, the same in pain and pleasure, forgiving ...
Meera remembers her grandmother's prayer shelf. A leaf, a flower, a little water. Nothing expensive. Just love, every single morning.
The third movement asks: what is real?
Chapter thirteen. The field and its knower.
Verse two.
This body, Kaunteya, is called the field. Whoever knows it is called the knower of the field by those who know.
And Krishna says: know me as the knower in every field. You are not the field. You are the one who sees it.
Chapter fourteen. The three gunas.
Verse five.
Sattva, rajas and tamas, the gunas born of nature, bind the imperishable embodied self to the body, mighty-armed one.

Guna also means a strand of rope. Sattva binds with attachment to happiness and knowledge. Rajas with craving and restless action. Tamas with carelessness, laziness and sleep. Whoever rises above all three, Krishna says, is free.
Chapter fifteen. The Supreme Person.
It begins with an upside-down tree. Verse one.
They speak of an imperishable sacred fig, its roots above and its branches below. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows it knows the Vedas.
Cut it, Krishna says, with the strong axe of detachment, and seek the source. And then: I am seated in the hearts of all.
Chapter sixteen. The divine and the demonic.
Fearlessness, truth and compassion on one side. Arrogance, anger and harshness on the other.
Then a warning that reads like a guide to every feed. Verse twenty-one.
Threefold is this gate of hell, the ruin of the self: desire, anger and greed. Therefore, give up these three.
Chapter seventeen. The three kinds of faith.
Food, worship, discipline and giving: each comes in three kinds, like the gunas. And at the centre, verse three.
Each person's faith follows their nature, Bharata. A person is made of faith: whatever one's faith is, that one is.
The chapter ends on three words that, by tradition, close every chapter of the Gita: Om, Tat, Sat.
Chapter eighteen. The yoga of liberation.
The longest chapter, seventy-eight verses, and it gathers everything.

Renunciation, Krishna says, is not giving up action. It is giving up attachment to its fruit. He repeats his advice from chapter three: better your own path, done imperfectly. And he says the Lord lives in the heart of every being.
And then, after seventeen chapters of teaching, he does something remarkable. He does not give Arjuna an order. Verse sixty-three.
Thus I have told you wisdom more secret than all secrets. Reflect on it fully, then do as you wish.
And then his last and most intimate word. Verse sixty-six.
Giving up all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins. Do not grieve.
Have you heard this with a focused mind, Krishna asks? Is your confusion gone? And Arjuna, who sat down with his bow at his feet, stands firm. Verse seventy-three.
My delusion is gone. By your grace, Achyuta, I have regained my memory. I stand firm, my doubts are gone. I will do as you say.
At six in the morning, Meera types her reply. We won't tell you which one she chose. That was never the point. She chose with a steady mind.
And Sanjaya, who has told the whole story to a blind king, ends it like this. Verse seventy-eight.
Wherever there is Krishna, the lord of yoga, and wherever there is Arjuna, the archer, there are fortune, victory, prosperity and sure justice. That is my conviction.
That was the Bhagavad Gita. All eighteen chapters. Next, we go chapter by chapter, starting with the one that answers overthinking.

iast: evam uktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśat |
visṛjya sa-śaraṃ cāpaṃ śoka-saṃvigna-mānasaḥ ||
1.47.en: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.
1.47.speaker: Sanjaya

iast: tam uvāca hṛṣīkeśaḥ prahasann iva bhārata |
senayor ubhayor madhye viṣīdantam idaṃ vacaḥ ||
2.10.en: Then, O Bharata, between the two armies, Hrishikesha, as if smiling, spoke these words to the one sinking in despair.
2.10.speaker: Sanjaya
2.10.gloss: hṛṣīkeśa = Krishna · bhārata: Sanjaya, telling the story to the blind king

iast: karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana |
mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr mā te saṅgo’stv akarmaṇi ||
2.47.en: Your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not cling to inaction.
2.47.speaker: Krishna

iast: śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt |
sva-dharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ para-dharmo bhayāvahaḥ ||
3.35.en: Better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's dharma done well. Better to die in your own dharma; another's dharma is full of fear.
3.35.speaker: Krishna

deva: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत ।
iast: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata |
abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmy aham ||
4.7.en: Whenever dharma declines, O Bharata, and adharma rises, then I bring myself forth.
4.7.speaker: Krishna

iast: paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām |
dharma-saṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
4.8.en: To protect the good, to destroy wrongdoing, and to establish dharma, I come into being, age after age.
4.8.speaker: Krishna

deva: ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः ।
iast: brahmaṇy ādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ |
lipyate na sa pāpena padma-patram ivāmbhasā ||
5.10.en: One who acts, offering every action to Brahman and giving up attachment, is not stained by sin, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
5.10.speaker: Krishna

iast: uddhared ātmanātmānaṃ nātmānam avasādayet |
ātmaiva hy ātmano bandhur ātmaiva ripur ātmanaḥ ||
6.5.en: Lift yourself up by yourself; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is its enemy.
6.5.speaker: Krishna

deva: मयि सर्वमिदं प्रोतं सूत्रे मणिगणा इव ॥ ७-७॥
iast: mattaḥ parataraṃ nānyat kiñcid asti dhanañjaya |
mayi sarvam idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva ||
7.7.en: There is nothing higher than me, Dhananjaya. All this is strung on me, like gems on a thread.
7.7.speaker: Krishna

iast: tasmāt sarveṣu kāleṣu mām anusmara yudhya ca |
mayy arpita-mano-buddhir mām evaiṣyasy asaṃśayaḥ ||
8.7.en: Therefore, at all times, remember me, and fight. With your mind and intellect offered to me, you will surely come to me.
8.7.speaker: Krishna

deva: पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति ।
iast: patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ toyaṃ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati |
tad ahaṃ bhakty-upahṛtam aśnāmi prayatātmanaḥ ||
9.26.en: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering, made with devotion by one whose heart is pure, I accept and partake of.
9.26.speaker: Krishna

iast: yad yad vibhūtimat sattvaṃ śrīmad ūrjitam eva vā |
tat tad evāvagaccha tvaṃ mama tejo’ṃśa-sambhavam ||
10.41.en: Whatever being is glorious, beautiful or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendour.
10.41.speaker: Krishna

deva: यदि भाः सदृशी सा स्याद्भासस्तस्य महात्मनः ॥ ११-१२॥
iast: divi sūrya-sahasrasya bhaved yugapad utthitā |
yadi bhāḥ sadṛśī sā syād bhāsas tasya mahātmanaḥ ||
11.12.en: If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth in the sky at once, it might resemble the splendour of that great being.
11.12.speaker: Sanjaya

iast: kālo’smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddho
lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ |
ṛte’pi tvāṃ na bhaviṣyanti sarve
ye’vasthitāḥ pratyanīkeṣu yodhāḥ ||
11.32.en: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds, come forth to consume the worlds. Even without you, none of the warriors arrayed in the opposing armies will remain.
11.32.speaker: Krishna

deva: अद्वेष्टा सर्वभूतानां मैत्रः करुण एव च ।
iast: adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānāṃ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca |
nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ kṣamī ||
12.13.en: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from 'mine' and from ego, the same in pain and pleasure, forgiving ...
12.13.speaker: Krishna
12.13.gloss: the sentence completes in 12.14: '... that devotee is dear to me'

deva: एतद्यो वेत्ति तं प्राहुः क्षेत्रज्ञ इति तद्विदः ॥ १३-२॥
iast: idaṃ śarīraṃ kaunteya kṣetram ity abhidhīyate |
etad yo vetti taṃ prāhuḥ kṣetrajña iti tad-vidaḥ ||
13.2.en: This body, Kaunteya, is called the field. Whoever knows it is called the knower of the field by those who know.
13.2.speaker: Krishna

iast: sattvaṃ rajas tama iti guṇāḥ prakṛti-sambhavāḥ |
nibadhnanti mahābāho dehe dehinam avyayam ||
14.5.en: Sattva, rajas and tamas, the gunas born of nature, bind the imperishable embodied self to the body, mighty-armed one.
14.5.speaker: Krishna

deva: छन्दांसि यस्य पर्णानि यस्तं वेद स वेदवित् ॥ १५-१॥
iast: ūrdhva-mūlam adhaḥ-śākham aśvatthaṃ prāhur avyayam |
chandāṃsi yasya parṇāni yas taṃ veda sa veda-vit ||
15.1.en: They speak of an imperishable sacred fig, its roots above and its branches below. Its leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows it knows the Vedas.
15.1.speaker: Krishna

iast: tri-vidhaṃ narakasyedaṃ dvāraṃ nāśanam ātmanaḥ |
kāmaḥ krodhas tathā lobhas tasmād etat trayaṃ tyajet ||
16.21.en: Threefold is this gate of hell, the ruin of the self: desire, anger and greed. Therefore, give up these three.
16.21.speaker: Krishna

deva: श्रद्धामयोऽयं पुरुषो यो यच्छ्रद्धः स एव सः ॥ १७-३॥
iast: sattvānurūpā sarvasya śraddhā bhavati bhārata |
śraddhā-mayo’yaṃ puruṣo yo yac-chraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ ||
17.3.en: Each person's faith follows their nature, Bharata. A person is made of faith: whatever one's faith is, that one is.
17.3.speaker: Krishna

iast: iti te jñānam ākhyātaṃ guhyād guhyataraṃ mayā |
vimṛśyaitad aśeṣeṇa yathecchasi tathā kuru ||
18.63.en: Thus I have told you wisdom more secret than all secrets. Reflect on it fully, then do as you wish.
18.63.speaker: Krishna

deva: अहं त्वा सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः ॥ १८-६६॥
iast: sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja |
ahaṃ tvā sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ ||
18.66.en: Giving up all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins. Do not grieve.
18.66.speaker: Krishna
18.66.gloss: schools read 'all dharmas' differently; every reading keeps the last words, mā śucaḥ: do not grieve

iast: naṣṭo mohaḥ smṛtir labdhā tvat-prasādān mayācyuta |
sthito’smi gata-sandehaḥ kariṣye vacanaṃ tava ||
18.73.en: My delusion is gone. By your grace, Achyuta, I have regained my memory. I stand firm, my doubts are gone. I will do as you say.
18.73.speaker: Arjuna

deva: यत्र योगेश्वरः कृष्णो यत्र पार्थो धनुर्धरः ।
iast: yatra yogeśvaraḥ kṛṣṇo yatra pārtho dhanur-dharaḥ |
tatra śrīr vijayo bhūtir dhruvā nītir matir mama ||
18.78.en: Wherever there is Krishna, the lord of yoga, and wherever there is Arjuna, the archer, there are fortune, victory, prosperity and sure justice. That is my conviction.
18.78.speaker: Sanjaya

shishya.show: śiṣyas te’haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam
shishya.en: I am your disciple; teach me, I have taken refuge in you

najayate.en: it is never born, nor does it ever die

vasamsi.en: as one casts off worn-out clothes

yajna.en: action other than for the sake of offering

yadyad.show: yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas tat tad evetaro janaḥ
yadyad.en: whatever the best do, others do

pranipata.en: by bowing, by asking, by serving

jnanagni.en: the fire of knowledge turns all karma to ash

padma.en: as a lotus leaf by water

samadarshi.en: the wise see the same in all

dipa.en: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker

raso.en: I am the taste in water

prabha.en: the light of moon and sun

yogakshema.en: I carry what they need and protect what they have

yatkaroshi.show: yat karoṣi yad aśnāsi yaj juhoṣi dadāsi yat
yatkaroshi.en: whatever you do, eat, offer, give

nantam.show: nāntaṃ na madhyaṃ na punas tavādiṃ
nantam.en: no end, no middle, no beginning

nadinam.en: as the many rivers rush to the sea

kshetrajnam.en: know me as the knower in every field

asanga.en: cutting it with the strong axe of detachment

hrdi.en: I am seated in the hearts of all

ahara.en: food too is of three kinds

tyaga.en: giving up the fruit of all action

hrddeshe.en: the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings
